reason: While the text does include specific ritual and ceremonial prescriptions—particularly regarding Passover observance (matzot, blood on doorposts, the lamb sacrifice) and Sabbath observance—these are consistently presented as expressions of covenant obedience and memorials to God's deliverance, not as ends in themselves. The recurring emphasis throughout the passage is on God's compassion for the suffering people, His mighty deeds of salvation (פָּקַד, הִצִּיל, נִשְׁמַר), and obedience to His laws and voice (שָׁמַע אֶל־קוֹלוֹ, שְׁמַר חֻקָּיו). When God states His expectations, He emphasizes relationship, covenant, justice, and moral obedience. The rituals function symbolically within this larger theological framework rather than representing what is intrinsically important to Yahweh. Additionally, Jethro's advice on judicial administration (chapters 17-18) demonstrates that ethical governance and justice—not ritual—are critical concerns.
